itineraries.title: Visayas Circuit: Cebu, Bohol and Siquijor in 14 Days
itineraries.subtitle: From Cebu's colonial streets to Bohol's chocolate hills and Siquijor's turquoise waterfalls, a journey through the central Visayas
itineraries.notes: Loop itinerary starting from Cebu. Ferries between islands (2–4 hours per crossing). Bring cash—ATMs are scarce outside Cebu City.
itineraries.climate: Best time: December to May (dry season), with temperatures of 26–32°C and constant humid heat. Avoid June to November: the southwest monsoon brings frequent rain and a risk of typhoons. The Visayas are less exposed than the northern Philippines but remain vulnerable in September–October.

visits.text: Cebu City is the Philippines' oldest city - this is where Magellan landed in 1521, and where he died just weeks later, killed by Chief Lapu-Lapu on Mactan Island across the strait. The city preserves traces of this turbulent history.

Fort San Pedro, built by the Spanish in 1565, is the country's oldest fort. It's a modest stone triangle steeped in history—it served as a Spanish garrison, a Japanese prison camp, and a zoo before being restored. The interior gardens are peaceful and shaded.

The Basilica of Santo Niño houses the Philippines' oldest Christian relic—a statuette of the Child Jesus given by Magellan in 1521. The church is always packed with devotees lighting candles and praying aloud. The atmosphere is intense and sincere.

Right next door, Magellan's Cross - or rather its shrine. The original cross planted by Magellan in 1521 is said to be inside a cross made of tindalo wood, itself protected by an octagonal pavilion with a painted ceiling. Historians debate its authenticity, but devotees don't care and come to pray.

activities.text: Stroll through Carbon Market, Cebu's largest and oldest market. It's loud, dense, chaotic - and fascinating. Mountains of mangoes, hundreds of dried fish, medicinal herbs, hardware goods. Not a tourist market, a real city market.

Lechon dinner in Cebu - the city considers itself the roast suckling pig capital of the Philippines. The skin crackles when you bite it, the meat is infused with herbs and lemongrass. Ask for a local restaurant rather than a chain.

visits.text: The Temple of Leah, in the hills above Cebu, is a neo-Roman mausoleum built by a businessman for his deceased wife. Corinthian columns, golden statues, monumental staircases - it's kitsch, grandiose and touching all at once. The view over the city from the terrace is worth the trip.

Continue climbing to Tops Lookout, the highest viewpoint accessible by vehicle above Cebu City. From the platform, the 360° panorama sweeps across the city, Cebu Strait, Mactan Island and the interior mountains. Best in late afternoon when the heat haze lifts.

The Taoist Temple, in the Beverly Hills residential district (yes, like Los Angeles), is a colorful Chinese temple open to visitors. Red and green pagodas, carved dragons, and a clear view over the city. Cebu's Chinese community is old and influential - this temple is its symbol.

activities.text: Evening at IT Park - Cebu's business district that comes alive at night. The call centers work on American hours, so restaurants and food courts stay open until 3am. Young, modern atmosphere, very different from the historic center.
If you like live music, Filipinos are formidable singers. Cebu's karaoke bars aren't tourist traps - it's genuine national culture. Any tricycle driver knows a good bar.

visits.text: Journey from Cebu City to Moalboal on the island's southwest coast—3 hours by bus or van through the mountains. The landscape shifts from dense city to jungle, then sugarcane fields and coastal villages.

Moalboal is a divers' village. No fine sandy beach here - the Panagsama shore is rocky and lined with bars and dive centers. What draws people is what's happening underwater: 5 meters from shore, the reef drops vertically into deep blue.

White Beach, 10 minutes by scooter from Panagsama, is Moalboal's real beach - white sand, coconut palms, calm water. Much less crowded than northern Cebu's beaches, it offers a simple and pleasant spot to relax.

activities.text: First snorkeling outing at Panagsama: enter the water from shore and swim 20 meters—you come upon the Sardine Run. A school of several million sardines forms a shifting silver wall right at the edge of the drop-off. The sardines constantly change shape like a single organism. It's free, accessible to everyone, and stunning.

practical_info.tip: Best early morning when the water is calm

activities.text: Dinner at one of Panagsama Beach's restaurants. The vibe is laid-back - divers comparing their days, solo travelers reading, reggae music in the background. The grilled fish is fresh and cheap.

visits.text: Pescador Island, 20 minutes by bangka from Moalboal, is a vegetation-covered rock sitting in the middle of the strait. Underwater, it's a cathedral: the reef descends in vertical walls carpeted with soft corals, gorgonians and sponges. Green turtles reside around the island year-round - you'll almost certainly encounter one.

Kawasan Falls, 30 minutes' drive south of Moalboal (Badian village), are among the Philippines' most beautiful. The turquoise water tumbles in two tiers into a jungle-surrounded pool. The water's almost surreal blue comes from the limestone it flows through.

activities.text: Canyoneering to Kawasan Falls - the region's star activity. You work your way up the canyon for 3-4 hours, jumping from rock to rock, swimming through natural pools and jumping off cliffs (3 to 15 meters) into turquoise water. Intense, wet, and memorable.

practical_info.booking: Guide required, book the day before
practical_info.tip: Water shoes essential, leave your belongings at the hotel

activities.text: Return to Moalboal exhausted but happy. One last snorkel at sunset with the sardines - the school moves differently depending on the time and light. At night, the sardines rise toward the surface and shimmer under the lights.

visits.text: Ferry from Cebu City to Tagbilaran, the capital of Bohol. The crossing takes 2 to 4 hours depending on the ferry. Tagbilaran is a small provincial city without much appeal, but it is the gateway to Bohol.

Baclayon Church, 6 km from Tagbilaran, is one of the Philippines' oldest - built of coral stone by Jesuits in 1596. The 2013 earthquake severely damaged it, but restoration is progressing. The adjacent museum displays religious artifacts from the colonial era.

The Loboc River winds through thick jungle in the interior of Bohol. Allow for a round trip by road from Tagbilaran to explore it. Coconut palms and stilt villages line its banks. It is one of the greenest and most peaceful landscapes in the Philippines.

activities.text: Lunch cruise on the Loboc River, reached by road from Tagbilaran. A floating restaurant boat travels upriver for an hour, with a Filipino buffet on board and local musicians. It is touristy but pleasant - the river is beautiful and the food decent.

practical_info.tip: Boats depart hourly, no need to book ahead

activities.text: Optional: stand-up paddleboarding or kayaking on the Loboc River, reached by road from Tagbilaran, a more authentic experience than the cruise. You paddle beneath the canopy, passing kingfishers and monitor lizards.

visits.text: The Chocolate Hills are Bohol's natural landmark - 1,268 grassy conical hills that turn chocolate brown in the dry season (hence the name). Plan a round trip by road from Tagbilaran to the Carmen viewpoint. The view is surreal: hundreds of identical domes stretch to the horizon like a giant model.

The tarsier sanctuary in Corella lets you observe these tiny primates (they fit in a hand). Tarsiers are nocturnal and extremely sensitive to noise and light. The sanctuary requires silence, bans flash photography, and limits visitor numbers. Respect the rules - stress can literally kill a tarsier.

The Man-Made Forest, a cathedral of mahogany trees planted in the 1950s, forms a green tunnel along 2 km of road between Loboc and Bilar. Plan a round trip by road from Tagbilaran. Light filters through the canopy - it is cool, quiet, and photogenic.

Sevilla's bamboo suspension bridge spans the Loboc River at a height of 25 meters. Plan a round trip by road from Tagbilaran. It sways when you walk on it - fun or terrifying depending on how you feel about heights. The view of the river below is worth the vertigo.

activities.text: Scooter tour through Bohol's interior. The roads are decent, traffic almost non-existent outside towns. You pass rice paddies, village churches, coconut groves, and children greeting you by shouting “Hey Joe!” (the nickname given to foreigners since the war).
Dinner in Tagbilaran - try kalamay, a local confection made from glutinous rice and coconut sugar, sold in coconut shells. It's Bohol's edible souvenir.

visits.text: Panglao, a small island connected to Bohol by two bridges, is where the beaches and resorts are concentrated. Plan a round trip by road from Tagbilaran to reach Alona Beach. Alona Beach, the best known, is a curve of white sand lined with restaurants and dive centers. It is Bohol's most developed beach—lively but not overwhelming.

Hinagdanan Cave, in Panglao's interior, hides a freshwater underground lake beneath a ceiling of stalactites. You descend a staircase into a chamber lit by natural skylights. Swimming is possible—the water is cool and green.

Balicasag Island, 45 minutes by bangka from Panglao, is a marine sanctuary. The coral drop-off surrounding the island is one of the Visayas' most spectacular - the reef plunges vertically into inky blue 3 meters from shore.

activities.text: Diving or snorkeling at Balicasag. Green turtles are everywhere, corals in excellent condition, and schools of surgeonfish form silver clouds at the drop-off edge. For certified divers, the descending wall is spectacular.
Dolphin watching off Panglao. Bangkas leave at dawn (5:30am) and regularly encounter groups of spinner dolphins. Not guaranteed, but frequent in dry season.

practical_info.tip: Very early departure, bring coffee to go

visits.text: Ferry from Tagbilaran to Siquijor—a 2-hour crossing. Siquijor is the most mysterious of the Visayas islands. Filipinos call it “the island of fire”: early Spanish navigators saw glows in the night (probably fireflies) and thought the island was haunted. Even today, Siquijor is renowned for its traditional healers and potions.
Siquijor Town, around the port, is tiny and peaceful. Saint Francis of Assisi Church, white and clean, dates from the 19th century.

Capilay Spring Park, reached by road from Siquijor Town, is a freshwater pool fed by a natural spring. Locals come to swim with their families on weekends. The water is cool and clear, and the park shaded - a simple, pleasant stop.

activities.text: Scooter tour to get a feel for the island. Siquijor is 20 km in diameter—the complete loop takes 2 hours without stopping. Along the coastal road, you pass deserted beaches, village churches and giant trees (the century-old balete tree), with views of Bohol and Negros.
Sunset from Paliton Beach on the west coast. A row of coconut palms leans over a narrow white sand beach—the island's most photogenic natural frame.

visits.text: Cambugahay Falls, in the island's interior, drop in three tiers into turquoise pools. Plan a round trip by road from Siquijor Town. Rope swings let you jump into the water from the bank - fun and refreshing. Access is easy, a 10-minute walk downhill.

The Balete Tree, a century-old banyan fig with sprawling aerial roots, shelters a natural pool at its base where small fish nibble dead skin from your feet (a natural fish spa). Plan a round trip by road from Siquijor Town. The tree is impressive—its roots form a network of organic columns.

Lazi's church and convent, built in 1857 from coral stone and hardwood, form one of the finest colonial complexes in the Visayas. Plan a round trip by road from Siquijor Town. The convent, enormous for such a small island, reflects the ambition of the Augustinian Recollects who administered the island.

Salagdoong Beach, on the east coast, is known for its jumping platforms - 5 and 10 meters above deep, clear water. Plan a round trip by road from Siquijor Town. Even if you do not jump, the beach is beautiful and the water perfect for snorkeling.

activities.text: If you're curious, ask to meet a traditional healer (mananambal). These practitioners use plants, prayers and rituals to treat physical and spiritual ailments. The healers' festival is held every Holy Week in San Antonio. Outside this period, meetings are possible but discreet—ask at your accommodation.
Swimming and relaxation at Cambugahay Falls, reached by road from Siquijor Town. In the afternoon, the crowds thin out and you will have the pools almost to yourself. Bring a picnic.

visits.text: Ferry from Siquijor to Dumaguete—a 1-hour crossing. Dumaguete is nicknamed “the city of kindness” (City of Gentle People). It's a lively university town but never stressful, with a pleasant waterfront boulevard and a restaurant and café scene driven by the student community.
Rizal Boulevard, the seafront promenade, is the heart of Dumaguete. Locals gather there in the evening to walk and eat. Food stalls serve inexpensive barbecue and vegetable tempura.

Silliman University, founded in 1901 by American Presbyterian missionaries, is Asia's oldest Protestant campus. The white period buildings, lawns and coconut wood church are worth a stroll - it's calm and shaded.

activities.text: Excursion to Apo Island, 45 minutes by bangka from Malatapay (30 min drive from Dumaguete). It's a 72-hectare marine sanctuary where green turtles are so numerous you sometimes see 10 in a single dive. Snorkeling from the beach is already excellent.

practical_info.booking: Departure from Malatapay market, can book through hotel

activities.text: Dinner on Rizal Boulevard. The waterfront terrace restaurants are affordable and the food is good - try kinilaw (Filipino ceviche with coconut vinegar).

visits.text: The Twin Lakes (Balinsasayao and Danao), 45 minutes into the mountains from Dumaguete, are two crater lakes nestled in dense rainforest at 900 meters elevation. The water is black and still, vegetation drips from the banks, the silence is total. You'd think you were in a different country.

Casaroro Falls, near the village of Valencia (20 min from Dumaguete), drop 30 meters into a narrow fern-covered canyon. From Valencia, continue by road to the trailhead. Access on foot involves a 300-step staircase, then a walk among rocks and river crossings - the climb back is demanding. The pool water is cold and the current strong - take care.

activities.text: Kayaking on Lake Balinsasayao. Kayaks are available for rent on site. You paddle on black, mirror-like water surrounded by tree ferns and birdsong. The second lake, Danao, is accessible via a 20-minute forest trail.

If it is Wednesday, visit Malatapay market, allowing for a round trip by road from Dumaguete. It is a noisy, colorful livestock and fish market - pigs, goats, dried fish, tropical fruit. Authentic and impressive.

visits.text: Ferry from Dumaguete to Liloan (south coast of Cebu), then drive north up the coast. Total journey to Cebu City takes 5-6 hours with stops.

Possible stop in Oslob. This is where whale sharks are fed by fishermen to allow tourists to swim with them. The site is controversial - feeding alters these wild animals' behavior and attracts massive crowds. If you go, know that the practice is criticized by marine conservation NGOs.
Alternative to Oslob: Sumilon Island, right across the water, offers a white sandbar surrounded by turquoise water and a preserved reef for snorkeling - without ethical controversy.

Heading back up to Cebu City, stop at the Simala Sanctuary (Monastery of the Holy Eucharist). This neo-Gothic church-fortress, perched in the hills, is a major pilgrimage site for Filipinos. The architecture is extravagant - turrets, stained glass, monumental staircases. A place of intense faith.

activities.text: Scenic drive along Cebu's southeast coast. The road winds between sea and mountains, passing fishing villages and viewpoints over the Bohol Strait.
Reunion dinner in Cebu City - the loop is complete. Return to lechon or discover satti (chicken and beef skewers in coconut sauce, a Mindanao specialty adopted by Cebu).

visits.text: Bus then ferry from Cebu City to Bantayan Island, northwest of Cebu - count on 5-6 hours total. Bantayan is the island where Filipinos themselves go when they want beaches without crowds. The sand is white and powdery, the water calm and warm, accommodations simple and cheap.

Sugar Beach in Santa Fe is the main beach—a kilometer of fine sand bordered by a few unobtrusive resorts. The water is so shallow you walk 100 meters before it reaches your waist. No jet-skis, no banana boats—just the sea.
The village of Bantayan Town, in the west of the island, has a 17th-century coral church (Saints Peter and Paul Church) and a lively fish market. The streets are quiet, tricycles rare, dogs numerous.

activities.text: Island scooter tour. Bantayan is 15 km long—in two hours you've seen everything: deserted beaches on the north side, mangroves on the east, fishing villages. Stop at Ogtong Cave, a cave with a natural pool of turquoise freshwater.
Walk along Kota Beach. The beach is narrow, but the view is open and the sky's colors spectacular.

visits.text: Return to Cebu from Bantayan - same ferry + bus route, 5-6 hours. If your flight is in the evening, you have time for one last stop on Mactan Island, across from Cebu City.

The Lapu-Lapu Shrine, on Mactan beach, marks the spot where the warrior chief killed Magellan on April 27, 1521. A bronze monument depicts Lapu-Lapu as a national hero - the Philippines' first resistance fighter against colonizers. Irony: right across from it, an obelisk honors Magellan. Both sides commemorated side by side.

Mactan's guitar factories: the island is the Philippines' main producer of handcrafted guitars. The workshops (Alegre, Lapu-Lapu Guitar) shape ukuleles and guitars from local wood - you can visit and buy directly.

activities.text: Last-minute shopping: dried mangoes from Cebu (the country's best), otap (flaky cookies), and rosquillos (dry donuts). Mactan-Cebu Airport is international—direct flights to Manila, Palawan, and several Asian cities.

seo.h1_title: Visayas Circuit: Cebu, Bohol and Siquijor in 14 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: The central Visayas in 14 days: the colonial history and lechon of Cebu, the millions of sardines at Moalboal, the Chocolate Hills and tarsiers of Bohol, the turquoise waterfalls and healers of Siquijor, the turtles of Apo Island and the crater lakes of Negros. A loop itinerary from Cebu, traveling from ferry to ferry through the most beautiful islands of the central Philippines.
seo.seo_hook: Cebu, Bohol, Siquijor: 14 days through the Visayas amid the Chocolate Hills, millions of sardines, turquoise waterfalls and sea turtles
featured_list: Moalboal: the Sardine Run, a school of millions of sardines just 5 meters from shore
Bohol: Chocolate Hills, tiny tarsiers and Loboc River cruise
Siquijor: Cambugahay waterfalls, traditional healers and mystical island
Apo Island: marine sanctuary where you swim with dozens of green turtles

places_taglines.PH::cebu: The Philippines' oldest city, where Spanish forts, sacred basilicas and crispy lechon meet
places_taglines.PH::moalboal: A divers' village where millions of sardines swim just a few strokes from shore
places_taglines.PH::tagbilaran: Gateway to Bohol, island of Chocolate Hills, tarsiers and the Loboc River
places_taglines.PH::siquijor: The Visayas' mystical island, famous for its healers, waterfalls and secret beaches
places_taglines.PH::dumaguete: A gentle university city by the strait, jumping-off point for Apo Island and the Twin Lakes
places_taglines.PH::bantayan: A powdery sand island off Cebu, a peaceful haven far from the tourist crowds

highlights: Moalboal Sardine Run: millions of sardines in a silver wall just 5m from shore
Kawasan Falls canyoneering: 4h of jumps and swimming through a turquoise canyon
Chocolate Hills: 1,268 conical hills viewed from Carmen viewpoint
Island-hopping by ferry: Cebu, Bohol, Siquijor and Dumaguete connected by boat

itineraries.title: Palawan Tour: Coron to Puerto Princesa in 12 Days
itineraries.subtitle: Hidden lagoons, wartime wrecks, karst cliffs and an underground river—the complete north-to-south journey across Palawan
itineraries.notes: Linear north-south route across Palawan. Manila-Busuanga flight on arrival, Puerto Princesa-Manila flight on departure. Factor in van transfers between stages (roads can be rough in places).
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: November to April, the dry season, with temperatures of 26–32°C and calm seas for boat transfers. Avoid June to October (monsoon, heavy daily rainfall, disrupted boat services). December–February offers the best balance between weather and crowds.

visits.text: Arrival at Busuanga Airport, a 30-minute drive from Coron Town. The van passes through countryside dotted with green hills and water buffalo before reaching the small town, wedged between the sea and karst cliffs. Coron is no beach resort—it's a fishing port that's adapted to tourism without losing its character.

Coron Town's market comes alive in late afternoon. Fishermen unload the day's catch—tuna, marlin, giant prawns—which the waterfront restaurants grill straight away for dinner. Try the local cashew nuts, a Palawan specialty, sold in bags on every street corner.

Coron's alleyways are simple - concrete, corrugated iron and hand-painted signs. But that authenticity is the charm. No international chains, no shopping malls. A few local bakeries (panaderias) sell sweet bread still warm for a handful of pesos.

activities.text: Climb the 721 steps of Mount Tapyas before sunset. The ascent is steep but short (20 minutes). At the summit, a white cross overlooks the entire bay of Coron—the karst islands stand silhouetted against a sky turning orange. It's the best viewpoint in the area, and it's free.

Grilled fish dinner on the waterfront. The restaurants lined up facing the harbor all work the same way: you choose your fish from the display, they grill it over charcoal. The price is negotiated by weight.

visits.text: Day trip by bangka (traditional outrigger boat) around Coron Island. First stop: Kayangan Lake. After a short climb over the karst rocks, the view of the lake below takes your breath away—a bowl of emerald water ringed by black cliffs draped in vegetation. The descent leads to a floating dock from which you dive into water so clear the bottom is visible at 15 meters.

Twin Lagoon, two pools of turquoise water connected by a narrow passage between the cliffs. At low tide, you swim through an opening in the rock; at high tide, you climb a wooden ladder and descend the other side. The water in the second pool is warmer - underground springs heat it.

Barracuda Lake, deeper and stranger. The water goes from 28°C at the surface to 38°C at depth - a mixture of fresh and salt water that creates convection currents visible to the naked eye. If you dive below 5 meters, the heat becomes palpable. The lake takes its name from a large solitary barracuda that used to live there.

Final stop at Coral Garden, a reef accessible by snorkeling from the bangka. The corals are in good condition and the variety of tropical fish is impressive - clownfish, damselfish, parrotfish, surgeonfish.

activities.text: Lunch served on the bangka between stops - rice, grilled fish, fruit. The boatmen prepare the meal on a small grill at the back of the boat while you swim. Simple and perfect.
Snorkeling at your own pace around the reefs. If you don't have your own equipment, the bangkas provide it—quality varies, so it's better to rent a good mask in Coron Town before the excursion.

visits.text: Coron is one of the best wreck diving sites in the world. In September 1944, the US Navy sank about a dozen Japanese ships sheltering in the bay. Several of these wrecks rest between 10 and 40 meters deep, accessible by scuba diving. The Irako, a 147-meter supply ship, and the Akitsushima, a seaplane tender, are the most impressive.

For non-divers, the Skeleton Wreck lies at a depth of just 5 meters—visible while snorkeling in calm weather. The hull overgrown with corals and sponges attracts schools of fish. It's a strange experience to float above a warship looking down through the water.
CYC Beach, a small white sand beach on an islet 20 minutes away by bangka, offers a break between dives. The water is calm, the bottom sandy, and the island barely 200 meters long.

activities.text: Scuba diving on one or two wrecks (for certified divers). Coron's dive centers offer full-day or half-day trips. Book the day before, especially in high season (December-March).

Late afternoon, head to Maquinit Hot Springs, 30 minutes by tuk-tuk from Coron Town. These hot saltwater springs (38-40°C) are nestled among the rocks by the sea. The main pool faces the sunset - a perfect moment of relaxation after a day of diving.

visits.text: The crossing from Coron to El Nido takes between 3 hours 30 minutes and 7 hours depending on the type of boat—speedboat or slow bangka. The open-sea journey can be rough, especially during the monsoon (June–October). If you get seasick, take the speedboat and medication before departure.

El Nido appears behind a curtain of black karst cliffs rising above the sea. The contrast is striking: vertical rock spires 200 meters high drop straight into turquoise water. The small town stretches along a beige sand beach lined with restaurants and dive shops.

Walk down El Nido's main street in late afternoon. It's lively without being overwhelming—tricycles (motorbikes with sidecars), stray dogs, children playing basketball on a concrete court, and travelers from around the world sitting at outdoor tables.

activities.text: Sunset from Corong-Corong Beach, a 10-minute tricycle ride south of El Nido. The beach is quieter than the one in the town center, and the view of the karst cliffs illuminated by the evening light is remarkable.

Dinner in one of the main street restaurants. Filipino cuisine is underrated - try the kare-kare (oxtail stew in peanut sauce) or sinigang (sour tamarind soup). Portions are generous and prices modest.

visits.text: A day of island hopping—Tour A, the most popular in El Nido. First stop: Big Lagoon, a sea inlet hemmed in by dizzyingly high cliffs. The bangka stops at the entrance and you continue by kayak through an increasingly narrow channel. The water shifts from navy blue to jade green in a matter of meters.

Small Lagoon, right next door. You access it by swimming under a rock arch. On the other side, an enclosed pool surrounded by karst walls—it feels like a movie set. Tropical fish swim between your legs in warm, transparent water.

Secret Lagoon, reached through a hole in the cliff. You swim through an opening in the rock and emerge onto a hidden mini-beach, enclosed by walls on all sides - a circle of white sand and turquoise water invisible from outside.
Shimizu Island, an islet planted with coconut palms and a coral reef accessible by snorkeling. Lunch is often served here - on the beach, in the shade of the trees.

activities.text: Kayaking in the Big Lagoon. Kayaks are available for rent on site—expect to pay 200–300 PHP. Paddle to the back of the lagoon where the water becomes so shallow you can see fish darting under the hull.
Snorkeling around Shimizu Island. The corals are colorful and well preserved, and visibility often exceeds 15 meters. Watch out for jellyfish.

visits.text: Nacpan Beach, 45 minutes by scooter north of El Nido along a rough road (improved in recent years but still bumpy in places). The detour is worth it: 4 kilometers of golden sand, lined with coconut palms.

At the end of Nacpan, a sandbar connects to the neighboring beach of Calitang - the famous Twin Beach. One side has choppy water (ocean side), the other is flat (bay side). You walk between the two waters on a strip of sand 50 meters wide.

Las Cabanas Beach, south of El Nido, is where travelers gather for sunset. A zipline connects the beach to a small islet opposite—a popular attraction, but optional. The beach itself is pleasant, with bars right on the sand.

activities.text: Scooter tour through El Nido's hinterland. Behind the coastal cliffs, the landscape changes: terraced rice fields, water buffalo in the paddies, villages of bamboo and corrugated iron where children wave as you pass. It's another face of Palawan, far from the turquoise lagoons.

practical_info.tip: International driving license theoretically required, rarely checked

activities.text: Sunset at Las Cabanas with a drink in a beach bar. The atmosphere is relaxed, the music mellow, and the sun drops behind the karst islets.

visits.text: The van journey from El Nido to Port Barton takes 3 to 4 hours on a road that crosses the Palawan jungle: dense tropical forest, rivers, isolated villages.

Port Barton is the antithesis of El Nido. A village of 200 inhabitants, a sandy beach lined with coconut palms, no nightlife. The wifi is unreliable. That is exactly what those who come here are looking for.
Walk along the main beach in late afternoon. Fishermen mend their nets, dogs sleep in the shade, a few travelers read in hammocks. At the end of the beach, a path leads to a small isolated cove.

activities.text: First swim in Port Barton bay. The water is calm, warm, and sea turtles regularly come to swim near the shore - especially early morning and late afternoon.
Dinner in one of the village's small eateries. The choice is limited but fresh: grilled fish, rice, stir-fried vegetables. Some evenings, a guitarist plays Filipino ballads under the stars.

visits.text: Bangka excursion around the Port Barton islands - the calm, intimate version of El Nido's island hopping. No crowds here: your bangka will often be the only one on site. Exotic Island, a white sandbar ringed with turquoise water, is the first stop.
The larger German Island has a shaded beach and a reef just a few swimming strokes away. The clownfish are so unafraid they come to inspect you up close. The water is stunningly clear.

Starfish Island takes its name from the starfish that populate the shallow waters around the islet. Don't take them out of the water (they die within minutes in the air) - observe them where they are, in 30 cm of water.

activities.text: Snorkeling around the islands. Port Barton's reefs are among the best-preserved in Palawan - less frequented than El Nido's, they harbor remarkable coral diversity. Green turtles frequently spotted.

practical_info.tip: Bring your own mask, borrowed ones are often in poor condition

activities.text: Lunch on a deserted beach, prepared by the boatman: grilled fish, green mango, rice. Feet in the sand, alone on the island.

visits.text: Head south toward Sabang—the starting point for Puerto Princesa's underground river, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999. The journey from Port Barton takes 4 to 5 hours by van, with the option of an overnight stop in Sabang or a day trip from Puerto Princesa (a 1-hour 30-minute drive).

Puerto Princesa's underground river extends 8.2 kilometers beneath a karst mountain—it's one of the longest navigable underground rivers in the world. The tour covers the first 1.5 kilometers in a rowboat. The guide illuminates the walls with a flashlight: stalactites, stalagmites, thousands of bats, and rock formations that resemble cathedrals.
Sabang Beach, right across from the boat landing, is a pleasant surprise. Fine sand, clear water, thick jungle in the background. Few people outside the river tour hours.

activities.text: Underground river tour by rowboat. Reserve your permit in advance—the number of visitors is limited to 900 per day. The tour lasts 45 minutes in near-total darkness, with the sound of water and the beating of bat wings lulling you along.

practical_info.booking: Permit required, book online or through your accommodation
practical_info.tip: Bring a hat, the bats fly over the boats

activities.text: Swimming at Sabang Beach after the tour. The water is warm, the bottom sandy, and monitor lizards (large lizards) stroll calmly on the beach - harmless but impressive.

visits.text: Puerto Princesa is Palawan's capital—a sprawling provincial city with no great architectural charm, but lively and functional. Restaurants, shops and local life are centered on the main street (Rizal Avenue). This is where you return to civilization after several days in isolated villages.
Puerto Princesa's central market is worth a visit in the morning. Tropical fruit in abundance (Palawan mangoes), dried fish, spices. The atmosphere is noisy and colorful.

Baker's Hill, on the outskirts of town, is a kitschy but enjoyable garden park, famous for its hopia (filled pastries) and cookies. Filipinos love it - it's an almost obligatory stop for them. The view over the valley from the terrace is pleasant.

activities.text: Excursion to Honda Bay, 30 minutes north of Puerto Princesa. Island hopping between three or four islets - Starfish Island, Luli Island, Cowrie Island. Less spectacular than Coron or El Nido, but the water is beautiful and the reefs alive.

practical_info.booking: Can be booked from the city

activities.text: Dinner on Rizal Avenue. Try the crocodile sisig (yes, chopped crocodile sisig-style) - a local specialty, a bit touristy but original. Otherwise, grilled chicken inasal is a Filipino classic that's always reliable.

visits.text: The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, in central Puerto Princesa, is a city landmark - white and blue façade, cool and quiet interior. Filipinos are deeply Catholic and the churches are rarely empty.

Take a tricycle to Iwahig, about 20 km from the city on this leg of the trip, a 35-minute drive. The river runs through dense mangroves that you explore by paddleboard or kayak. The ecosystem is rich—herons, kingfishers, mangrove crabs. It is calm, green, and the opposite of the turquoise blue of the previous days.

The Palawan Butterfly Eco-Garden, a small botanical garden on the outskirts of town, houses butterflies endemic to Palawan and a collection of medicinal plants used by indigenous peoples. A short but instructive visit.

activities.text: Firefly watching on the Iwahig River at dusk. By boat, you go up the river in darkness - and the mangroves light up. Thousands of fireflies blink in synchrony in the trees, like living fairy lights. It's an astonishing natural spectacle, especially in the dry season.

Last Filipino dinner. If you haven't tried lechon (spit-roasted suckling pig) yet, now's the time. The skin is crisp as glass, and the meat melts in your mouth. It's the ultimate celebration dish in the Philippines.

visits.text: Last morning in Puerto Princesa. If your flight is in the afternoon, take advantage of the morning to stroll one last time along Rizal Avenue. The sidewalks are lively from 7am - vendors selling pan de sal (warm bread rolls), local coffee stands, schoolchildren in uniform.

Puerto Princesa airport is 5 minutes from the city center. Direct flights to Manila (1 hour 20 minutes), Cebu (1 hour 30 minutes) or Clark. If you are continuing to the Visayas, the flight to Cebu saves you going back through Manila.

activities.text: Last purchases: Palawan cashew nuts (the best in the country), dried mangoes, and why not a bottle of lambanog (coconut liquor). The souvenir shops on Rizal Avenue charge fair prices.

seo.h1_title: Palawan Tour: Coron to Puerto Princesa in 12 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: Palawan north to south in 12 days: the karst lagoons and wartime wrecks of Coron, El Nido's cliffs and secret beaches, the timeless village of Port Barton, and the UNESCO-listed underground river at Puerto Princesa. A linear route that crosses the Philippines' most beautiful island without retracing your steps.
seo.seo_hook: Four destinations, twelve days: the complete Palawan traverse through lagoons, shipwrecks, jungle and a UNESCO underground river
featured_list: Coron: Kayangan Lake, Twin Lagoon and diving on the 1944 Japanese wrecks
El Nido: karst cliffs, Big Lagoon and 4 km of sand at Nacpan Beach
Port Barton: intimate island hopping and sea turtles
Puerto Princesa: UNESCO underground river and synchronous fireflies of Iwahig

places_taglines.PH::el-nido: Towering limestone karsts plunging into turquoise lagoons, gateway to the Bacuit archipelago
places_taglines.PH::port-barton: A timeless fishing village with no paved roads or ATMs, facing a pristine lagoon
places_taglines.PH::puerto-princesa: Palawan's laid-back capital, launching point for the UNESCO-listed underground river

highlights: Coron → El Nido boat crossing: spectacular journey between karst islands
Kayangan Lake: one of the Philippines' most beautiful lakes, ringed by cliffs
Puerto Princesa Underground River: 8 km beneath the mountain, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999
Port Barton: Palawan's best-kept secret, between El Nido and Puerto Princesa

itineraries.title: Philippines Grand Tour: Rice Terraces, Lagoons and the Visayas in 21 Days
itineraries.subtitle: From Manila to Banaue's millennia-old rice terraces, from Palawan's lagoons to the Visayas' reefs and Siargao's waves—three weeks across the archipelago
itineraries.notes: Grand tour covering three regions: Northern Luzon (rice terraces), Palawan (lagoons), and the Visayas (reefs and waterfalls). Allow for 5–6 domestic flights. Fast-paced itinerary—for travelers who want to see as much as possible in three weeks.
itineraries.climate: Best time: December to April, the dry season with temperatures of 26–32°C and maximum sunshine. Avoid June to October: the southwest monsoon brings daily torrential rain and a risk of typhoons (peaking in August–September). May gets very hot and humid; November remains uncertain with the remnants of typhoons.

visits.text: Manila is a city you either love or flee—loud, dense, chaotic, yet full of surprises. Intramuros, the old city fortified by the Spanish in the 16th century, is the best starting point. Stone walls encircle a district of quiet alleys, churches, and shaded courtyards—an island of silence within the megacity.

Fort Santiago, at the entrance to Intramuros, served as the Spanish citadel and later as a Japanese prison during the war. José Rizal, the Philippine national hero, was imprisoned here before his execution in 1896. The museum traces his final hours — his writings, his footsteps marked from the cell to the execution site.

San Agustin Church, built in 1607, is the oldest stone church in the Philippines and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The interior is sumptuous: a trompe-l'oeil ceiling, crystal chandeliers, and a granite floor imported from China. It survived earthquakes, typhoons, and the 1945 bombardment.

Rizal Park (Luneta Park) stretches out facing Manila Bay. This is where Rizal was executed by firing squad in 1896—a granite monument marks the spot. Filipinos come here to jog in the morning, picnic with family on weekends, and watch the sunset in the evening.

activities.text: Calesa ride through Intramuros — a horse-drawn carriage tour along the cobbled streets. Touristy but pleasant for covering the district without walking in the heat. Negotiate the price before you climb aboard.

Filipino dinner: adobo (chicken or pork braised in vinegar and soy), sinigang (sour tamarind soup), and halo-halo (shaved ice dessert with beans, jellies, and condensed milk). Halo-halo looks bizarre at first glance and becomes addictive after the first spoonful.

visits.text: Binondo, Manila's Chinatown, is the oldest Chinatown in the world—founded in 1594. The narrow streets overflow with restaurants, apothecaries, temples, and jewelry shops. Taste the siopao (filled steamed buns), lumpia (Filipino spring rolls), and pancit canton (stir-fried noodles).

Quiapo Church houses the Black Nazarene, a black wooden statue of Christ carrying the cross. On January 9, several million barefoot devotees pull the statue through the streets—one of the world's largest religious processions. Outside the festival, the church remains a place of intense devotion.

The National Museum of Fine Arts, in a neoclassical building facing Rizal Park, displays Juan Luna's Spoliarium — a monumental 7-by-4-meter canvas that won the gold medal at the 1884 Paris Salon. Admission is free.

activities.text: In the evening, explore Poblacion in Makati—the former working-class neighborhood that has become the heart of Manila's nightlife. Rooftop bars, fusion restaurants, and art galleries in former garages. The vibe is young and creative.
Sunset over Manila Bay from the waterfront or from a rooftop bar in Makati. The Manila sky takes on spectacular orange hues - pollution has at least that one advantage.

visits.text: The journey from Manila to Banaue is an adventure in itself—a 9-hour overnight bus ride through Luzon's cordillera. The bus leaves Manila in the evening and arrives in Banaue at dawn, in Ifugao province. You wake up at altitude, surrounded by green mountains and mist.

The Banaue Rice Terraces have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. Carved into the mountain slopes by the Ifugao people over 2,000 years ago, they rise 1,500 meters up the hillsides. The earth and stone walls, maintained by hand, represent an engineering feat that has endured for millennia.

Banaue's main viewpoint, five minutes from town by tricycle, offers the classic panoramic view of the terraces. Early morning, when the rice paddies are shrouded in mist, the landscape feels otherworldly. If the terraces are flooded (planting season, February-March), the sky's reflection in the water adds another dimension.

Banaue's small museum displays Ifugao farming tools, woven textiles, and wooden sculptures (bulul, guardians of rice granaries). It's modest but instructive for understanding the culture that created these terraces.

activities.text: Rest and acclimatization after the night bus. Banaue sits at 1,200 meters elevation — the air is cool morning and evening (15-20°C), a welcome contrast after Manila's heat. Grab a coffee at one of the small downtown restaurants.
Ifugao dinner: red rice from the terraces (local variety with a nutty taste) accompanied by pinikpikan — chicken broth prepared using the traditional method. Ifugao cuisine is simple and comforting.

visits.text: Batad is the hidden jewel of the rice terraces—a natural amphitheater of terraces forming a semicircle, more spectacular and better preserved than Banaue. Access is via a 45-minute downhill trail from the saddle point (the jeepneys' departure point). The path crosses rice paddies where farmers work with their feet in the mud.

Batad village is a handful of wooden and corrugated iron houses clinging to the slope. No road, no cars — everything's done on foot. Ifugao families have lived in the same thatch-roofed houses for generations. Some offer homestays: a mat on the floor, a meal of red rice and vegetables, and mountain silence.

Tappiya Falls, accessible from Batad via a steep 40-minute downhill trail (and just as long uphill—be ready for a leg workout), drops 21 meters into a cold-water pool amid the jungle. The swim after the hike is a relief.

activities.text: Rice terrace trek with a local guide. The trail winds between terraces, crosses low stone walls, and follows millennia-old irrigation channels. The guide explains the hydraulic system, planting rituals, and the contemporary challenges facing Ifugao farmers.

practical_info.tip: Local guide required, hiking boots recommended

activities.text: Quiet evening in Batad. Little or no Wi-Fi, no bars, no noise—just roosters crowing, water murmuring through the channels, and stars above the terraces.

visits.text: Climb back up from Batad to the saddle point (45 min of steep ascent in the morning - leave early to avoid the heat), then jeepney to Banaue. If you have the energy, make a detour to the Hapao rice terraces in Hungduan, about one hour by road from Banaue, less well known but just as beautiful - and almost deserted.

Visit to an Ifugao weaving workshop. Village women weave on backstrap looms — an ancestral technique. The textiles with red and black geometric patterns tell stories of war, fertility, and social status.
Last look at the terraces from Banaue viewpoint in late afternoon. The low-angle light carves shadows into the terraces — it's the best time for photos.

activities.text: Meeting with an Ifugao family if your guide can arrange it. The elders share stories of life in the rice fields, cañao rituals (a community celebration), and the fragile balance between tradition and modernity. Young people leave for Manila, and maintaining the terraces takes manpower.
Overnight bus back to Manila (departs late afternoon, arrives early morning). You'll connect directly to your flight to Palawan.

visits.text: Flight Manila → Busuanga (1 hour). You trade the misty mountains of Luzon for the karst islands of Palawan in sixty minutes. In Coron, the rhythm shifts dramatically—from a packed bus to a bangka gliding across the water.
Settle into Coron Town and explore the harbor. Bangkas lined up along the waterfront await tomorrow's excursions. The fish market comes alive in late afternoon—tuna, mahi-mahi, giant shrimp.
Climb Mount Tapyas (721 steps) for sunset. 360-degree views over the bay, islands, and karst cliffs glowing red in the evening light.

activities.text: Grilled fish dinner on the waterfront. You choose your fish from the stall, they grill it over charcoal. Simple, fresh, cheap.

visits.text: Day trip by bangka: Kayangan Lake (emerald lake ringed by cliffs—Coron's postcard scene), Twin Lagoon (two pools connected by a passage under the rock), Barracuda Lake (water with a thermocline, warm at depth). Three exceptional sites in one day.

The Skeleton Wreck, a Japanese WWII shipwreck lying at a depth of 5 meters, is visible while snorkeling. The coral-covered hull attracts schools of fish. In 1944, American aircraft sank a dozen Japanese ships here—Coron is now one of the world's best wreck diving destinations.
Maquinit Hot Springs at the end of the day—saltwater pools at 38°C, tucked among rocks at the sea's edge. The sunset from the pools is perfect.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Coral Garden between stops. The corals are intact and the variety of tropical fish impressive.
Lunch on the bangka between sites — rice, grilled fish, fruit. The boatmen cook on a small grill at the stern.

visits.text: Speedboat Coron → El Nido (3 hours 30 minutes). El Nido's karst cliffs rise from the sea like black teeth—Palawan's most spectacular scenery.

Afternoon: bangka trip from El Nido. Big Lagoon (kayaking between the cliffs), Small Lagoon (swimming under a rock arch), Secret Beach (a beach hidden behind the rock). Three unreal landscapes in a few hours.

activities.text: Kayaking in the Big Lagoon. You paddle through an increasingly narrow channel between 200-meter cliffs. The water shifts from navy blue to jade green.
Sunset from El Nido beach or Corong-Corong beach. The karst cliffs are silhouetted against an orange sky.

visits.text: Nacpan Beach, 45 minutes by scooter north of El Nido: 4 kilometers of almost deserted golden sand. No jet skis—just coconut palms, a few thatched huts, and the ocean.
Las Cabanas Beach on the way back for sunset. Beach bars, relaxed vibe, views of the karst islets.

activities.text: Scooter ride through El Nido's backcountry: rice paddies, water buffalo, bamboo villages. Another face of Palawan, far from the lagoons.
Flight El Nido → Cebu the next morning (via Manila or Clark depending on the carrier). End of the Palawan chapter, beginning of the Visayas.

visits.text: Arrival in Cebu, the oldest city in the Philippines. Fort San Pedro (1565), Basilica del Santo Niño (the country's oldest Christian relic), and Magellan's Cross — the entire historic center can be explored on foot in half a day.
Carbon Market, Cebu's largest market — loud, dense, authentic. Mountains of mangoes, dried fish, medicinal herbs.

activities.text: Lechon dinner (roast suckling pig) — Cebu is the lechon capital of the Philippines. Crispy skin, herb-infused meat.
Evening at IT Park—the district that comes alive at night thanks to call centers running on American hours.

visits.text: Drive to Moalboal (3 hours). The Sardine Run: enter the water from Panagsama Beach, swim 20 meters—a wall of several million sardines rises before you. Free, accessible, stunning.
Pescador Island, 20 minutes by bangka. Vertiginous coral drop-off, resident green turtles, cascading soft corals.

activities.text: Canyoneering at Kawasan Falls (Badian, 30 min south): 4 hours of jumping, swimming, and climbing through a turquoise-water canyon. Intense and memorable.
Relaxed evening in Panagsama — grilled fish restaurants, divers swapping stories.

visits.text: Ferry Cebu → Tagbilaran (2–4 hours). Inland tour of Bohol: Chocolate Hills (1,268 conical hills, brown in the dry season, about 51 km from Tagbilaran, 1 hour by road), Corella tarsier sanctuary (silence and no flash), Man-Made Forest (2 km tunnel of mahogany trees).
Lunch cruise on the Loboc River, about 26 km from Tagbilaran, 35 minutes by road. Filipino buffet on a floating boat that heads up a river lined with jungle and coconut palms. Touristy but pleasant.

activities.text: Scooter tour through Bohol's interior — rice paddies, village churches, kids waving hello.
Dinner in Tagbilaran. Try kalamay, a local confection made from sticky rice and coconut sugar.

visits.text: Balicasag Island, a marine sanctuary 45 minutes by bangka from Panglao. Spectacular coral drop-off, green turtles everywhere. For certified divers, the descending wall is a highlight.
Alona Beach on Panglao, about 20 km from Tagbilaran, 25 minutes by road—white sand, dive centers, seafront restaurants. The most developed beach in Bohol.
Hinagdanan Cave: an underground lake beneath a ceiling of stalactites, lit by natural skylights. A cool swim in a mysterious setting.

activities.text: Diving or snorkeling at Balicasag. Schools of surgeonfish, turtles, corals in excellent condition.
Dolphin watching off Panglao at dawn (5:30am). Common in dry season.

visits.text: Ferry Tagbilaran → Siquijor (2 hours). The mystical island of the Visayas—known for its healers, fireflies, and unique atmosphere. Complete scooter circuit (20 km in diameter, 2 hours without stopping).
Cambugahay Falls: three tiers of turquoise water, rope swings for launching into the pools. Siquijor's most refreshing spot.
The Balete Tree—a century-old fig tree with sprawling roots and a natural fish-spa pool at its base. Strange and photogenic.
Lazi Church and Convent (1857), built of coral stone—one of the most beautiful colonial complexes in the Visayas.

activities.text: Sunset at Paliton Beach—a row of coconut palms leaning over white sand, the island's most photogenic shot.
Salagdoong Beach for jumping enthusiasts: platforms at 5 and 10 meters above deep, clear water.

visits.text: A slower day on Siquijor. The Tubod Marine Sanctuary is a small protected reef accessible by snorkeling from the beach. Colorful fish, intact corals, and almost nobody around.
San Juan village, on the west coast, is the island's (modest) tourist hub. A few restaurants, beachfront accommodations, and white sand beaches.

If curiosity draws you, ask to meet a traditional healer (mananambal). These practitioners use plants, prayers, and rituals to heal body and spirit. The healers' festival takes place every Holy Week in San Antonio.

activities.text: A day of relaxation and beach time. After two weeks at a fast pace, Siquijor is the ideal island to slow down. Read, swim, sleep in a hammock. Nothing is mandatory.
Dinner on San Juan beach. At the restaurants, you can eat grilled fish and kinilaw (Filipino ceviche with coconut vinegar) with your feet in the sand.

visits.text: Flight from Dumaguete or Cebu to Siargao (via Manila or Cebu — connections vary, check ahead). Siargao is the Philippines' surf capital, but it's also a beautiful island for non-surfers: lagoons, mangroves, deserted islets.
General Luna, the main village, is a single street lined with restaurants, surf shops, and bars. The vibe recalls Canggu in Bali 10 years ago — relaxed, young, international, not yet overrun.

Cloud 9, 10 minutes from General Luna by scooter, is Siargao's legendary surf spot. A hollow wave breaking over a coral reef — reserved for experienced surfers. From the wooden boardwalk, you watch surfers charge the wave. Even without surfing, the show is worth it.

activities.text: If you surf, this is the moment. Cloud 9 for advanced surfers, neighboring beaches (Jacking Horse, Stimpy's) for intermediates. Surf lessons are offered everywhere for beginners—the inside waves are mellow and accessible.
Sunset from a General Luna bar. Live music, cocktails, friendly atmosphere — Siargao in the evening is a surf village where everyone knows each other after two days.

visits.text: Sugba Lagoon, in the island's northwest, is a turquoise lagoon ringed by mangroves. Access is by bangka from Del Carmen (45 min drive + 30 min boat). Jumping platforms (10 meters) let you dive into the warm, calm water. Paddleboarding, kayaking, and snorkeling available onsite.

The Magpupungko Rock Pools, on the east coast, about 45 minutes by road from General Luna, are natural pools that only appear at low tide. Flat rock formations create basins of crystal-clear water in the middle of the reef - you swim in a natural aquarium. Check the tide times before setting off.

activities.text: Scooter ride on the Coconut Road, a route that crosses kilometers of coconut plantations in the island's center. The palms form a tunnel of greenery — it's one of the Philippines' most beautiful roads and it's nearly deserted.
Late afternoon surf session or a swim at your leisure. Siargao's pace is slow—no one will rush you.

visits.text: Island hopping: Siargao's three islands. Naked Island is a bare sandbar in the middle of the ocean—no trees, no shade, just white sand and blue water. Bring a hat.
Daku Island, the largest of the three, offers coconut palms for shade and a living reef for snorkeling. This is where lunch happens — fishermen grill the morning catch on the beach.
Guyam Island, a tiny islet of coconut palms (you can walk around it in 5 minutes), is Siargao's postcard scene. A tropical version of Robinson Crusoe.

activities.text: Snorkeling around all three islands. The reefs are alive and colorful, fish abundant.
Last sunset in Siargao. The golden light on the coconut palms, the sound of waves, distant music from a bar — this is the moment to realize that three weeks in the Philippines isn't enough.

visits.text: Flight Siargao → Manila (1.5–2 hours depending on connections). Return to the megacity after three weeks of islands and villages. The shock is abrupt—traffic jams, horns, urban heat. But Manila has its own energy that you come to appreciate.

If you have a few hours before your international flight, Greenbelt in Makati is an air-conditioned shopping mall with gardens where you can eat, drink coffee, and buy last-minute souvenirs in modern comfort.

activities.text: Last Filipino meal: back to halo-halo to come full circle. Or adobo, sinigang, lechon — everything you discovered in three weeks, one last time.
Transfer to NAIA airport. Allow plenty of time—the trip from Manila to the airport can take 2 hours in rush-hour traffic.

seo.h1_title: Philippines Grand Tour: Rice Terraces, Lagoons and the Visayas in 21 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: Three weeks across the Philippines, from Manila to Banaue's millennia-old rice terraces, from Palawan's karst lagoons to the Visayas' reefs and Siargao's waves. A grand tour crossing four regions and nine islands to see the best of the archipelago in a single trip.
seo.seo_hook: Four regions, nine islands, 21 days: UNESCO rice terraces, Coron lagoons, Moalboal sardines, and Siargao surf in one circuit
featured_list: Banaue & Batad: 2,000-year-old terraced rice fields, UNESCO World Heritage
Coron: Kayangan Lake, Japanese wrecks from 1944, and hot springs
Moalboal: The Sardine Run, millions of sardines 5 meters from shore
Siargao: Cloud 9, Sugba Lagoon, and island hopping among deserted islets

highlights: Overnight bus Manila → Banaue: 9 hours through Luzon's cordillera
Speedboat Coron → El Nido: spectacular crossing between karst islands
Kawasan canyoneering: 4 hours of jumps through a canyon of turquoise water
Cloud 9 in Siargao: Philippine surfing's legendary wave
